pairs.source_text: Frequenter hortatus es, ut epistulas, si quas paulo curatius scripsissem, colligerem publicaremque. Collegi non servato temporis ordine, neque enim historiam componebam, sed ut quaeque in manus venerat.
pairs.question: Quo ordine Plinius epistulas suas se collegisse in prooemio profitetur?
pairs.question_en: In what order does Pliny declare, in his preface, that he collected his letters?
pairs.answer_en: Not keeping the order of time.
pairs.derivation: The programmatic opening of the Epistulae: the collection is deliberately not chronological, because it is not history. Anchored to Pliny + his letter-collection; single verifiable answer stated verbatim (non servato temporis ordine). Closed-book: one of the best-known facts about the published corpus of Pliny's letters.

pairs.source_text: edendum autem ex pluribus causis, maxime quod libelli quos emisimus dicuntur in manibus esse, quamvis iam gratiam novitatis exuerint; nisi tamen auribus nostris bibliopolae blandiuntur.
pairs.question: Quos Plinius suspicatur auribus suis blandiri, cum libelli eius in manibus hominum esse dicantur?
pairs.question_en: Whom does Pliny suspect of flattering his ears when his books are said to be in people's hands?
pairs.derivation: The Roman book trade: the bibliopolae who report an author's sales. Anchored to Pliny + his published libelli; one-word answer stated verbatim. Closed-book and culturally salient: the bookseller is the standard figure of Roman publication (cf. Martial, Horace).

pairs.source_text: Temptavi enim imitari Demosthenen semper tuum, Calvum nuper meum, dumtaxat figuris orationis.
pairs.question: Quos duos oratores Plinius se figuris orationis imitatum esse scribit?
pairs.question_en: Which two orators does Pliny say he imitated in figures of speech?
pairs.derivation: Pliny's declared models in oratory. Anchored to Pliny + the named orators; both names stated verbatim. Closed-book literary-culture fact: the Greek-and-Roman pairing (Demosthenes with Licinius Calvus) is the standard canon of Atticist models.

pairs.source_text: Quid agit Comum, tuae meaeque deliciae? quid suburbanum amoenissimum, quid illa porticus verna semper, quid platanon opacissimus, quid euripus viridis et gemmeus, quid subiectus et serviens lacus?
pairs.question: Quod oppidum Plinius et Caninium Rufum communes delicias appellat?
pairs.question_en: Which town does Pliny call the shared delight of himself and Caninius Rufus?
pairs.derivation: Comum, the patria of both Pliny and his friend Caninius Rufus, on the lake. Anchored to the two named men; single place-name answer stated verbatim. Closed-book: Pliny's origin at Comum, and his benefactions there, are ambient knowledge about him.

pairs.source_text: Rustici Aruleni periculum foverat, exsultaverat morte; adeo ut librum recitaret publicaretque, in quo Rusticum insectatur atque etiam 'Stoicorum simiam' appellat, adicit 'Vitelliana cicatrice stigmosum'.
pairs.question: Quo convicio Regulus Arulenum Rusticum in libro suo appellavit?
pairs.question_en: By what insult did Regulus call Arulenus Rusticus in his book?
pairs.derivation: Regulus' notorious pamphlet against Arulenus Rusticus, executed under Domitian. Anchored to the two named men; the phrase is quoted verbatim. Closed-book: the jibe 'Stoicorum simia' is among the best-remembered slurs of the Domitianic delatores.

pairs.source_text: Subiunxit egregiam causam: 'Scripsit' inquit 'in epistula quadam, quae apud Domitianum recitata est: "Regulus, omnium bipedum nequissimus"'; quod quidem Modestus verissime scripserat.
pairs.question: Quibus verbis Mettius Modestus Regulum in epistula apud Domitianum recitata notavit?
pairs.question_en: With what words did Mettius Modestus brand Regulus in a letter read out before Domitian?
pairs.answer_en: The wickedest of all two-legged creatures.
pairs.derivation: Modestus' famous phrase about the informer Regulus. Anchored to Modestus + Regulus + Domitian; quoted verbatim. Closed-book: 'omnium bipedum nequissimus' is a proverbially cited insult from Pliny.

pairs.source_text: Nitebamur nos in parte causae sententia Metti Modesti optimi viri: is tunc in exsilio erat, a Domitiano relegatus.
pairs.question: A quo principe Mettius Modestus in exsilium relegatus erat?
pairs.question_en: By which emperor had Mettius Modestus been relegated into exile?
pairs.derivation: Modestus' exile under Domitian, the background to Regulus' trap-question in court. Anchored to the named man; single named answer stated verbatim. Closed-book: the Domitianic exiles are standard shared history.

pairs.source_text: lacerat Herennium Senecionem tam intemperanter quidem, ut dixerit ei Mettius Carus 'Quid tibi cum meis mortuis? Numquid ego Crasso aut Camerino molestus sum?' quos ille sub Nerone accusaverat.
pairs.question: Quos duos viros Regulus sub Nerone accusaverat, ut Plinius refert?
pairs.question_en: Which two men had Regulus prosecuted under Nero, according to Pliny?
pairs.derivation: Regulus' career as a Neronian delator, thrown at him by his rival informer Mettius Carus. Anchored to Regulus + Nero; two named answers stated verbatim. Closed-book: Regulus' victims are part of the standard record of the informers.

pairs.source_text: Evigilaveram; nuntius a Spurinna: 'Venio ad te.' 'Immo ego ad te.' Coimus in porticum Liviae, cum alter ad alterum tenderemus.
pairs.question: In qua porticu Plinius et Spurinna, dum alter ad alterum tendit, congressi sunt?
pairs.question_en: In which portico did Pliny and Spurinna meet as each was making for the other?
pairs.derivation: The porticus Liviae on the Esquiline, one of the standard public promenades of Rome. Anchored to the two named men; single named monument stated verbatim. Closed-book: the portico is a well-known Augustan monument of the city.

pairs.source_text: Ridebis, et licet rideas. Ego, ille quem nosti, apros tres et quidem pulcherrimos cepi.
pairs.question: Quot apros Plinius Cornelio Tacito se cepisse scribit?
pairs.question_en: How many boars does Pliny write to Cornelius Tacitus that he caught?
pairs.derivation: The celebrated hunting letter to Tacitus. Anchored to Pliny + Tacitus; a single number stated verbatim (apros tres). Closed-book: the 'three boars caught beside the nets, with notebook in hand' is among the most quoted scenes in the Epistulae.

pairs.source_text: Ad retia sedebam; erat in proximo non venabulum aut lancea, sed stilus et pugillares; meditabar aliquid enotabamque, ut si manus vacuas, plenas tamen ceras reportarem.
pairs.question: Quae instrumenta Plinius pro venabulo aut lancea ad retia sedens secum habuit?
pairs.question_en: What implements did Pliny have by him at the hunting-nets instead of a boar-spear or lance?
pairs.derivation: The stylus and wax tablets carried to the hunt in place of weapons. Anchored to Pliny + the hunt of 1.6; both objects named verbatim. Closed-book and culturally salient: the pugillares are the everyday Roman writing kit, and this is the letter that made the image famous.

pairs.source_text: Proinde cum venabere, licebit auctore me ut panarium et lagunculam sic etiam pugillares feras: experieris non Dianam magis montibus quam Minervam inerrare.
pairs.question: Quas duas deas Plinius pariter per montes errare dicit, cum venatori pugillares ferendos suadet?
pairs.question_en: Which two goddesses does Pliny say roam the mountains alike, when he urges a hunter to carry writing-tablets?
pairs.derivation: Diana as goddess of the hunt paired with Minerva as goddess of study. Anchored to the named deities and their canonical spheres; both named verbatim. Closed-book: the divine attributions are shared Roman knowledge, and the epigram is a much-quoted line.

pairs.source_text: Paene praeterii, quod minime praetereundum fuit, accepisse me careotas optimas, quae nunc cum ficis et boletis certandum habent.
pairs.question: Cum quibus duobus cibis careotae Plinio missae certare dicuntur?
pairs.question_en: With which two foods are the dates sent to Pliny said to compete?
pairs.derivation: Careotae (the choice Syrian date), figs and boleti as the standard gift-foods and delicacies. Anchored to Pliny's letter of thanks; both foods named verbatim. Closed-book food culture: dates, figs and boleti are canonical Roman table items (cf. Martial's Xenia).

pairs.source_text: Petiturus sum enim ut rursus vaces sermoni quem apud municipes meos habui bibliothecam dedicaturus.
pairs.question: Qua de causa Plinius apud municipes suos illum sermonem habuit?
pairs.question_en: On what occasion did Pliny deliver that speech before his fellow townsmen?
pairs.answer_en: When he was about to dedicate a library.
pairs.derivation: Pliny's dedication of a public library at Comum, one of his best-known municipal benefactions. Anchored to Pliny + his municipes; the occasion is stated verbatim. Closed-book: civic euergetism (library, alimenta) is the standard shape of a Roman notable's giving.

pairs.source_text: Accedebat his causis, quod non ludos aut gladiatores sed annuos sumptus in alimenta ingenuorum pollicebamur.
pairs.question: Quid Plinius municipibus suis pro ludis aut gladiatoribus pollicitus est?
pairs.question_en: What did Pliny promise his townsmen instead of games or gladiators?
pairs.answer_en: Yearly sums for the support of freeborn children.
pairs.derivation: Pliny's alimentary foundation at Comum, contrasted with the usual gift of games. Anchored to Pliny + his municipium; the promise is stated verbatim. Closed-book: the alimenta for freeborn children are a famous institution of Trajan's age and of Pliny in particular.

pairs.source_text: Etenim hunc ipsum sermonem non apud populum, sed apud decuriones habui, nec in propatulo sed in curia.
pairs.question: Apud quos et quo loco Plinius sermonem de munificentia sua habuit?
pairs.question_en: Before whom and in what place did Pliny deliver his speech about his own munificence?
pairs.answer_en: Before the decurions, in the council-house.
pairs.derivation: The municipal senate (decuriones) meeting in the curia, as opposed to a public address to the populus. Anchored to Pliny's speech at Comum; both facts stated verbatim. Closed-book institutional fact about Italian town government.

pairs.source_text: Satius est enim, ut Atilius noster eruditissime simul et facetissime dixit, otiosum esse quam nihil agere.
pairs.question: Quid Atilius, ut Plinius refert, satius esse dixit quam nihil agere?
pairs.question_en: What did Atilius say, as Pliny reports, is better than doing nothing?
pairs.derivation: The much-quoted epigram on otium versus idleness, attributed by Pliny to his friend Atilius. Anchored to the named speaker and reported by Pliny; the saying is quoted verbatim. Closed-book: the tag 'satius est otiosum esse quam nihil agere' circulates as a Latin proverb.

pairs.source_text: Multa claraque exempla sunt; sufficeret unum, Euphrates philosophus. Hunc ego in Syria, cum adulescentulus militarem, penitus et domi inspexi, amarique ab eo laboravi.
pairs.question: In qua provincia Plinius adulescens militans Euphraten philosophum cognovit?
pairs.question_en: In which province did Pliny, serving as a young soldier, come to know the philosopher Euphrates?
pairs.derivation: Pliny's military tribunate in Syria and his acquaintance there with the Stoic Euphrates. Anchored to Pliny + Euphrates; single place-name stated verbatim. Closed-book: Euphrates is a well-known Stoic of the period (also in Epictetus and Philostratus), and Syria is Pliny's known military posting.

pairs.source_text: At hoc ipsum scribe, nihil esse quod scribas, vel solum illud unde incipere priores solebant: 'Si vales, bene est; ego valeo.'
pairs.question: Qua formula priores Romani epistulas incipere solebant, ut Plinius refert?
pairs.question_en: With what formula did earlier Romans customarily begin their letters, as Pliny reports?
pairs.answer_en: 'If you are well, that is good; I am well.'
pairs.derivation: The standard opening formula of the Roman letter (abbreviated S.V.B.E.E.V.). Anchored to Roman epistolary custom as reported by Pliny; quoted verbatim. Closed-book and strongly culturally salient: the formula is the recognized shape of a Latin letter's greeting.

pairs.source_text: Increverat valetudo, quam temperantia mitigare temptavit; perseverantem constantia fugit. Iam dies alter tertius quartus: abstinebat cibo. Misit ad me uxor eius Hispulla communem amicum C. Geminium cum tristissimo nuntio, destinasse Corellium mori nec aut suis aut filiae precibus inflecti.
pairs.question: Quo genere mortis Corellius Rufus vitam finivit?
pairs.question_en: By what kind of death did Corellius Rufus end his life?
pairs.derivation: The voluntary death by abstinence of the consular Corellius Rufus. Anchored to the named man; the manner is stated verbatim (sponte... abstinebat cibo). Closed-book: death by inedia is the recognized Roman philosophical exit, and Corellius' is one of its famous instances.

pairs.source_text: Tertio et tricensimo anno, ut ipsum audiebam, pedum dolore correptus est. Patrius hic illi; nam plerumque morbi quoque per successiones quasdam ut alia traduntur.
pairs.question: Quoto anno aetatis Corellium Rufum pedum dolore correptum esse Plinius scribit?
pairs.question_en: In what year of his life does Pliny say Corellius Rufus was seized by gout?
pairs.derivation: The onset of Corellius' hereditary gout. Anchored to the named man; a single number stated verbatim. Closed-book: the long martyrdom to gout is the defining fact of Corellius' biography as Pliny transmits it.

pairs.source_text: Implevit quidem annum septimum et sexagensimum, quae aetas etiam robustissimis satis longa est.
pairs.question: Quotum annum Corellius Rufus impleverat cum decederet?
pairs.question_en: What year of life had Corellius Rufus completed when he died?
pairs.derivation: Corellius' age at death. Anchored to the named man; a single number stated verbatim. Closed-book biographical fact of the kind Roman readers carried about notable consulars.

pairs.source_text: Veni ad eum Domitiani temporibus in suburbano iacentem. Servi e cubiculo recesserunt, habebat hoc moris, quotiens intrasset fidelior amicus; quin etiam uxor quamquam omnis secreti capacissima digrediebatur. Circumtulit oculos et 'Cur' inquit 'me putas hos tantos dolores tam diu sustinere? ut scilicet isti latroni vel uno die supersim.'
pairs.question: Cui principi, quem latronem appellabat, Corellius Rufus vel uno die superesse cupiebat?
pairs.question_en: Which emperor, whom he called a bandit, did Corellius Rufus wish to outlive by even a single day?
pairs.derivation: Corellius' declared reason for enduring his agony: to survive Domitian. Anchored to Corellius + the emperor named in the same passage (Domitiani temporibus); the 'latro' is identified by the letter's own frame. Closed-book: the anecdote is a standard illustration of senatorial hatred of Domitian.

pairs.source_text: Magnum proventum poetarum annus hic attulit: toto mense Aprili nullus fere dies, quo non recitaret aliquis.
pairs.question: Quo mense, ut Plinius scribit, nullus fere dies sine alicuius recitatione fuit?
pairs.question_en: In which month, as Pliny writes, was there scarcely a day without someone giving a recitation?
pairs.derivation: The recitation season at Rome. Anchored to Pliny's report + the named month; stated verbatim. Closed-book and culturally salient: the public recitatio is the central institution of Roman literary life, and this is its classic description.

pairs.source_text: At hercule memoria parentum Claudium Caesarem ferunt, cum in Palatio spatiaretur audissetque clamorem, causam requisisse, cumque dictum esset recitare Nonianum, subitum recitanti inopinatumque venisse.
pairs.question: Quis imperator, clamore in Palatio audito, ad Nonianum recitantem subito venisse fertur?
pairs.question_en: Which emperor is said to have come suddenly upon Nonianus while he was giving a recitation, after hearing a shout on the Palatine?
pairs.derivation: The anecdote of Claudius dropping in unannounced on the historian Servilius Nonianus' recitation. Anchored to the emperor + the reciting author; both named verbatim. Closed-book: a standard illustration of the older, more eager audience for recitations.

pairs.source_text: Qui quidem diu quaerendus fuisset, nisi paratus et quasi provisus esset Minicius Acilianus, qui me ut iuvenis iuvenem, est enim minor pauculis annis, familiarissime diligit, reveretur ut senem.
pairs.question: Quem iuvenem Plinius Iunio Maurico fratris filiae maritum commendavit?
pairs.question_en: Which young man did Pliny recommend to Junius Mauricus as a husband for his brother's daughter?
pairs.derivation: Pliny's marriage-brokering for the daughter of Arulenus Rusticus, at the request of his brother Junius Mauricus. Anchored to the named parties; the candidate is named verbatim. Closed-book: the letter is the classic Roman document of how a match was arranged and what was weighed.

pairs.source_text: Patria est ei Brixia, ex illa nostra Italia quae multum adhuc verecundiae frugalitatis, atque etiam rusticitatis antiquae, retinet ac servat.
pairs.question: Ex quo municipio oriundus erat Minicius Acilianus, quem Plinius maritum commendavit?
pairs.question_en: From which town did Minicius Acilianus, whom Pliny recommended as a husband, come?
pairs.derivation: Brixia (Brescia) in Transpadane Italy, praised for old-fashioned frugality. Anchored to the named man; single place-name stated verbatim. Closed-book: the moral reputation of Transpadane Italy is a shared Roman commonplace to which Pliny himself belongs.

pairs.source_text: Pater Minicius Macrinus, equestris ordinis princeps, quia nihil altius volvit; allectus enim a Divo Vespasiano inter praetorios honestam quietem huic nostrae, ambitioni dicam an dignitati? constantissime praetulit.
pairs.question: A quo principe Minicius Macrinus inter praetorios allectus est?
pairs.question_en: By which emperor was Minicius Macrinus enrolled among the ex-praetors?
pairs.derivation: Adlection inter praetorios, the emperor's promotion of an equestrian into senatorial rank. Anchored to the named man + emperor; stated verbatim. Closed-book institutional fact about how the senate was replenished under the Flavians.

pairs.source_text: Habet aviam maternam Serranam Proculam e municipio Patavio. Nosti loci mores: Serrana tamen Patavinis quoque severitatis exemplum est.
pairs.question: Cuius municipii severos mores Plinius commemorat, cum Serranam Proculam laudat?
pairs.question_en: Whose town's strict morals does Pliny recall when he praises Serrana Procula?
pairs.derivation: The proverbial severity of Patavium (Padua). Anchored to the named woman + town; stated verbatim. Closed-book: Patavine strictness is a Roman commonplace (cf. Martial 11.16, and Livy's 'Patavinitas').

pairs.source_text: Paratae erant lactucae singulae, cochleae ternae, ova bina, halica cum mulso et nive.
pairs.question: Cum quibus rebus halicam in cena sua paratam Plinius memorat?
pairs.question_en: With what does Pliny record that the spelt-porridge at his dinner was served?
pairs.derivation: Halica (emmer groats) served with mulsum and chilled with snow. Anchored to Pliny's described menu; stated verbatim. Closed-book food culture: mulsum as the standard aperitif-wine and snow as the Roman means of chilling are ambient dining knowledge.

pairs.source_text: Audisses comoedos vel lectorem vel lyristen vel, quae mea liberalitas, omnes.
pairs.question: Quae acroamata Plinius convivae suo audienda paraverat?
pairs.question_en: What performers had Pliny provided for his guest to hear at dinner?
pairs.answer_en: Comic actors, a reader, and a lyre-player.
pairs.derivation: The three standard forms of Roman dinner entertainment. Anchored to Pliny's invitation-letter; all three named verbatim. Closed-book: comoedi, lector and lyristes are the recognized repertoire of the Roman convivium.

pairs.source_text: At tu apud nescio quem ostrea vulvas echinos Gaditanas maluisti.
pairs.question: Quas saltatrices Plinius convivam suum apud alium hospitem praetulisse queritur?
pairs.question_en: Which dancing-girls does Pliny complain his guest preferred at somebody else's house?
pairs.derivation: The Gaditanae, the notorious Spanish dancers of Roman dinner parties. Anchored to Pliny's reproach; named verbatim. Closed-book and culturally salient: the dancers of Gades are a fixed item of Roman luxury dining (cf. Martial, Juvenal).

pairs.source_text: Praeterea facit versus, quales Catullus meus aut Calvus, re vera quales Catullus aut Calvus.
pairs.question: Quorum duorum poetarum similes versus Pompeium Saturninum facere Plinius dicit?
pairs.question_en: Whose verses, of which two poets, does Pliny say Pompeius Saturninus' resemble?
pairs.derivation: Catullus and Licinius Calvus as the paired canon of Roman light verse. Anchored to the named contemporary poet; both models named verbatim. Closed-book literary-culture fact: the Catullus-Calvus pairing is the standard shorthand for the neoteric manner.

pairs.source_text: Legit mihi nuper epistulas; uxoris esse dicebat. Plautum vel Terentium metro solutum legi credidi.
pairs.question: Quibus duobus comicis poetis Plinius illas epistulas comparavit, quas Pompeius Saturninus uxoris esse dicebat?
pairs.question_en: To which two comic poets did Pliny compare the letters that Pompeius Saturninus said were his wife's?
pairs.derivation: Plautus and Terence as the canon of pure conversational Latin. Anchored to the named letters and their reader; both poets named verbatim. Closed-book: the two comedians are the standard Roman touchstone for idiomatic speech.

pairs.source_text: Est adhuc curae hominibus fides et officium, sunt qui defunctorum quoque amicos agant. Titinius Capito ab imperatore nostro impetravit, ut sibi liceret statuam L. Silani in foro ponere.
pairs.question: Cuius viri statuam Titinius Capito in foro ponere a principe impetravit?
pairs.question_en: Whose statue did Titinius Capito obtain the emperor's leave to set up in the forum?
pairs.derivation: The rehabilitation of the Neronian victim L. Silanus by a statue in the Forum, licensed by the emperor. Anchored to the two named men; stated verbatim. Closed-book: honorific statues in the Forum, and the need for imperial permission, are shared civic knowledge.

pairs.source_text: Est omnino Capitoni in usu claros viros colere; mirum est qua religione quo studio imagines Brutorum Cassiorum Catonum domi ubi potest habeat.
pairs.question: Quorum virorum imagines Titinius Capito domi colebat?
pairs.question_en: Whose portrait-busts did Titinius Capito keep and revere at home?
pairs.answer_en: Those of the Bruti, the Cassii, and the Catos.
pairs.derivation: The domestic cult of the republican heroes among the senatorial opposition. Anchored to the named man; the three families named verbatim. Closed-book and culturally salient: the imagines of Brutus, Cassius and Cato are the recognized emblems of libertas under the principate.

pairs.source_text: Nam iudicium centumvirale differri nullo modo, istuc aegre quidem sed tamen potest.
pairs.question: Quod iudicium Romae nullo modo differri posse Plinius scribit?
pairs.question_en: Which court's hearing does Pliny say can by no means be postponed at Rome?
pairs.derivation: The centumviral court, whose sittings admitted no adjournment. Anchored to the named tribunal; stated verbatim. Closed-book institutional fact: the centumviri are the great civil (inheritance) court and Pliny's own arena.

pairs.source_text: Esse autem tibi centum milium censum, satis indicat quod apud nos decurio es.
pairs.question: Quantum censum apud Plinii municipes decurionem habere oportebat?
pairs.question_en: What property qualification did a decurion among Pliny's townsmen have to possess?
pairs.derivation: The municipal census requirement for a town councillor. Anchored to Romatius Firmus + Comum; the figure is stated verbatim. Closed-book institutional fact about the graded property qualifications of Roman society.

pairs.source_text: Igitur ut te non decurione solum verum etiam equite Romano perfruamur, offero tibi ad implendas equestres facultates trecenta milia nummum.
pairs.question: Quantam pecuniam Plinius Romatio Firmo ad equestres facultates implendas obtulit?
pairs.question_en: How much money did Pliny offer Romatius Firmus to make up the equestrian property qualification?
pairs.derivation: Pliny's gift topping up a townsman's census from 100,000 to the equestrian 400,000. Anchored to the two named men; the sum is stated verbatim. Closed-book: the equestrian census of 400,000 HS and the patron's topping-up gift are shared Roman social knowledge.

pairs.source_text: Idem pro Cluentio ait se totam causam vetere instituto solum perorasse, et pro C. Cornelio quadriduo egisse.
pairs.question: Quot diebus Cicero pro C. Cornelio egisse dicitur?
pairs.question_en: For how many days is Cicero said to have pleaded on behalf of Gaius Cornelius?
pairs.derivation: Cicero's four-day defence of C. Cornelius, contrasted with the single-handed peroration pro Cluentio. Anchored to Cicero + the named client; the number is stated verbatim. Closed-book: the length of Cicero's great pleadings is standard rhetorical-historical knowledge.

pairs.source_text: Ideo in optima quaque mille figuras extemporales invenimus, in iis etiam quas tantum editas scimus, ut in Verrem: 'artificem quem? quemnam? recte admones; Polyclitum esse dicebant.'
pairs.question: Cuius artificis nomen Cicero in Verrem quasi ab alio admonitus profert?
pairs.question_en: Which artist's name does Cicero produce in the Verrines as though prompted by someone?
pairs.derivation: The famous extemporary figure in the Verrines. Anchored to Cicero's speech; the sculptor is named verbatim. Closed-book: Polyclitus is a canonical Greek sculptor and this is a much-cited rhetorical example.

pairs.source_text: Nec me praeterit summum oratorem Periclen sic a comico Eupolide laudari.
pairs.question: Qui comicus poeta Periclem oratorem laudavisse apud Plinium refertur?
pairs.question_en: Which comic poet is reported by Pliny to have praised Pericles as an orator?
pairs.derivation: Eupolis' celebrated lines on Pericles' persuasive sting. Anchored to Pericles + the named comic poet; stated verbatim. Closed-book: Eupolis on Pericles is a standard citation in ancient rhetorical criticism.

pairs.source_text: Perturbat me longa et pertinax valetudo Titi Aristonis, quem singulariter et miror et diligo. Nihil est enim illo gravius sanctius doctius, ut mihi non unus homo sed litterae ipsae omnesque bonae artes in uno homine summum periculum adire videantur. Quam peritus ille et privati iuris et publici!
pairs.question: Quem virum Plinius et privati iuris et publici peritissimum praedicat?
pairs.question_en: Which man does Pliny proclaim most learned in both private and public law?
pairs.derivation: Titus Aristo, the jurist of Trajan's age cited in the Digest. Anchored to Pliny + the description of his legal learning; the name is stated verbatim. Closed-book: Aristo is one of the named jurists of the classical age of Roman law.

pairs.source_text: Plurimum refert, quid esse tribunatum putes, inanem umbram et sine honore nomen an potestatem sacrosanctam, et quam in ordinem cogi ut a nullo ita ne a se quidem deceat. Ipse cum tribunus essem, erraverim fortasse qui me esse aliquid putavi, sed tamquam essem abstinui causis agendis.
pairs.question: Quo magistratu fungens Plinius causis agendis abstinuit?
pairs.question_en: While holding which magistracy did Pliny abstain from pleading cases?
pairs.derivation: The sacrosanct tribunate and the incompatibility Pliny felt between it and standing as an advocate. Anchored to Pliny + the named office; stated verbatim. Closed-book: the tribune's sacrosanctitas and precedence are shared knowledge of Roman public law.

pairs.source_text: Tranquillus contubernalis meus vult emere agellum, quem venditare amicus tuus dicitur.
pairs.question: Cui contubernali suo Plinius agellum empturo apud Baebium Hispanum favit?
pairs.question_en: Which of his companions did Pliny support with Baebius Hispanus when he wished to buy a small estate?
pairs.derivation: Pliny's patronage of the biographer Suetonius, here in a property purchase. Anchored to Pliny + Baebius Hispanus; Suetonius is named verbatim. Closed-book: Suetonius' place in Pliny's circle is a well-known fact of Latin literary history.

pairs.source_text: Post aliquot annos insigne atque etiam memorabile populi Romani oculis spectaculum exhibuit publicum funus Vergini Rufi, maximi et clarissimi civis, perinde felicis.
pairs.question: Quod genus funeris Verginio Rufo populus Romanus exhibuit?
pairs.question_en: What kind of funeral did the Roman people give Verginius Rufus?
pairs.derivation: The funus publicum decreed for Verginius Rufus. Anchored to the named man; stated verbatim. Closed-book: the state funeral is a recognized Roman honour, and Verginius' is its famous late instance.

pairs.source_text: Huius viri exsequiae magnum ornamentum principi magnum saeculo magnum etiam foro et rostris attulerunt. Laudatus est a consule Cornelio Tacito; nam hic supremus felicitati eius cumulus accessit, laudator eloquentissimus.
pairs.question: Quis consul Verginium Rufum in funere publico laudavit?
pairs.question_en: Which consul delivered the funeral eulogy of Verginius Rufus?
pairs.derivation: Tacitus as consul pronouncing the laudatio funebris over Verginius Rufus in AD 97. Anchored to both named men; stated verbatim. Closed-book: this is the best-attested public act of the historian Tacitus' career.

pairs.source_text: Triginta annis gloriae suae supervixit; legit scripta de se carmina, legit historias et posteritati suae interfuit. Perfunctus est tertio consulatu, ut summum fastigium privati hominis impleret, cum principis noluisset.
pairs.question: Quotiens Verginius Rufus consulatum gessit?
pairs.question_en: How many times did Verginius Rufus hold the consulship?
pairs.derivation: Verginius' third consulship as the summit open to a private citizen, after refusing the principate. Anchored to the named man; stated verbatim (tertio consulatu). Closed-book: Verginius' refusal of empire and his three consulships are standard imperial history.

pairs.source_text: Annum tertium et octogensimum excessit in altissima tranquillitate, pari veneratione. Usus est firma valetudine, nisi quod solebant ei manus tremere, citra dolorem tamen.
pairs.question: Quem annum aetatis Verginius Rufus excessit?
pairs.question_en: What year of his life had Verginius Rufus passed?
pairs.derivation: Verginius' great age at death. Anchored to the named man; the number is stated verbatim. Closed-book biographical fact about one of the most celebrated consulars of the age.

pairs.source_text: Nam cum vocem praepararet acturus in consulatu principi gratias, liber quem forte acceperat grandiorem, et seni et stanti ipso pondere elapsus est. Hunc dum sequitur colligitque, per leve et lubricum pavimentum fallente vestigio cecidit coxamque fregit.
pairs.question: Quod membrum Verginius Rufus fregit, cum librum elapsum colligere conaretur?
pairs.question_en: What did Verginius Rufus break when he tried to pick up the book that had slipped from his hands?
pairs.derivation: The accident that led to Verginius' death while he was rehearsing his consular speech of thanks. Anchored to the named man; stated verbatim. Closed-book: the manner of his final injury is the memorable detail of the story, and the speech of thanks (gratiarum actio) is itself a fixed consular duty.

pairs.source_text: Quin etiam in hac novissima valetudine, veritus ne forte inter quinqueviros crearetur, qui minuendis publicis sumptibus iudicio senatus constituebantur, cum illi tot amici senes consularesque superessent, me huius aetatis per quem excusaretur elegit.
pairs.question: Ad quam rem quinqueviri iudicio senatus constituebantur, inter quos Verginius Rufus creari verebatur?
pairs.question_en: For what purpose were the boards of five appointed by the senate's decision, among whom Verginius Rufus feared to be chosen?
pairs.derivation: The senatorial commission of five for cutting public expenditure under Nerva. Anchored to Verginius + the senate; the commission's purpose is stated verbatim. Closed-book institutional fact about the fiscal reform of the late 90s.

pairs.source_text: primum quod utrique eadem regio, municipia finitima, agri etiam possessionesque coniunctae, praeterea quod ille mihi tutor relictus affectum parentis exhibuit.
pairs.question: Quo munere Verginius Rufus in Plinium pupillum functus est?
pairs.question_en: In what capacity did Verginius Rufus act toward the young Pliny?
pairs.derivation: Verginius Rufus appointed Pliny's tutor. Anchored to both named men; stated verbatim (tutor relictus). Closed-book: tutela of a fatherless minor is a central Roman institution, and this guardianship is a standard fact of Pliny's biography.

pairs.source_text: Magna Isaeum fama praecesserat, maior inventus est. Summa est facultas copia ubertas; dicit semper ex tempore, sed tamquam diu scripserit. Sermo Graecus, immo Atticus.
pairs.question: Qua lingua Isaeus rhetor, quem Plinius laudat, declamabat?
pairs.question_en: In what language did the rhetorician Isaeus, whom Pliny praises, declaim?
pairs.answer_en: In Greek, and indeed Attic Greek.
pairs.derivation: Isaeus, the Greek declaimer who drew Roman audiences, speaking pure Attic and always extempore. Anchored to the named man; stated verbatim. Closed-book: the visiting Greek sophist is a fixture of Roman intellectual life under the empire.

pairs.source_text: Numquamne legisti, Gaditanum quendam Titi Livi nomine gloriaque commotum ad visendum eum ab ultimo terrarum orbe venisse, statimque ut viderat abisse?
pairs.question: Cuius scriptoris fama commotus Gaditanus quidam ab ultimo terrarum orbe Romam venisse dicitur?
pairs.question_en: Moved by the fame of which writer is a man of Gades said to have come to Rome from the ends of the earth?
pairs.derivation: The famous anecdote of the Spaniard who travelled from Gades merely to look at Livy. Anchored to Livy + the man of Gades; stated verbatim. Closed-book: the story is a standard illustration of Livy's fame in his own lifetime.

pairs.source_text: nisi vero falsum putamus illud Aeschinis, qui cum legisset Rhodiis orationem Demosthenis admirantibus cunctis, adiecisse fertur: 'ti de, ei autou tou thêriou êkousate;'
pairs.question: Cuius oratoris orationem Aeschines exsul Rhodiis recitasse fertur?
pairs.question_en: Whose speech is Aeschines said to have read out to the Rhodians in exile?
pairs.derivation: Aeschines in exile at Rhodes reading Demosthenes' speech and asking what if they had heard the beast himself. Anchored to the two named orators + Rhodes; stated verbatim. Closed-book: the anecdote is a canonical illustration of delivery (actio) in ancient rhetoric.

pairs.source_text: cumque vivente eo nubenti tibi in dotem centum milia contulerim, praeter eam summam quam pater tuus quasi de meo dixit, erat enim solvenda de meo, magnum habes facilitatis meae pignus, cuius fiducia debes famam defuncti pudoremque suscipere.
pairs.question: Quantam pecuniam Plinius Calvinae nubenti in dotem contulit?
pairs.question_en: How much money did Pliny contribute as dowry for Calvina when she married?
pairs.derivation: Pliny's dowry gift to his kinswoman Calvina, alongside his remission of her father's debt. Anchored to Pliny + Calvina; the sum is stated verbatim. Closed-book: the dos, provided by kin for a bride, is a central Roman institution.

pairs.source_text: Nam sibi et paucis opima quaedam, ceteris vilia et minuta ponebat. Vinum etiam parvolis lagunculis in tria genera discripserat, non ut potestas eligendi, sed ne ius esset recusandi, aliud sibi et nobis, aliud minoribus amicis, nam gradatim amicos habet, aliud suis nostrisque libertis.
pairs.question: In quot genera ille hospes, apud quem Plinius cenavit, vinum convivis discripserat?
pairs.question_en: Into how many grades had the host at whose house Pliny dined divided the wine for his guests?
pairs.derivation: The graded dinner: different wine for the host and chief guests, for lesser friends, and for freedmen. Anchored to the described dinner-party; the number is stated verbatim. Closed-book and culturally salient: the ranked convivium is a standing Roman social scandal (cf. Martial, Juvenal).

pairs.source_text: Here a senatu Vesticio Spurinnae principe auctore triumphalis statua decreta est, non ita ut multis, qui numquam in acie steterunt, numquam castra viderunt, numquam denique tubarum sonum nisi in spectaculis audierunt, verum ut illis, qui decus istud sudore et sanguine et factis assequebantur. Nam Spurinna Bructerum regem vi et armis induxit in regnum, ostentatoque bello ferocissimam gentem, quod est pulcherrimum victoriae genus, terrore perdomuit.
pairs.question: Cui genti Vestricius Spurinna regem vi et armis restituit?
pairs.question_en: To which people did Vestricius Spurinna restore a king by force of arms?
pairs.derivation: Spurinna's German campaign, for which the senate voted him a triumphal statue. Anchored to the named man + the named people; stated verbatim. Closed-book: the Bructeri are one of the standard German nations of Roman ethnography.

pairs.source_text: Here a senatu Vesticio Spurinnae principe auctore triumphalis statua decreta est, non ita ut multis, qui numquam in acie steterunt, numquam castra viderunt, numquam denique tubarum sonum nisi in spectaculis audierunt, verum ut illis, qui decus istud sudore et sanguine et factis assequebantur. Nam Spurinna Bructerum regem vi et armis induxit in regnum, ostentatoque bello ferocissimam gentem, quod est pulcherrimum victoriae genus, terrore perdomuit.
pairs.question: Quod praemium senatus, principe auctore, Vestricio Spurinnae decrevit?
pairs.question_en: What reward did the senate, on the emperor's motion, decree to Vestricius Spurinna?
pairs.derivation: The ornamenta triumphalia in statue form, the standard substitute for a triumph under the principate. Anchored to Spurinna + the senate; stated verbatim. Closed-book institutional fact: since Augustus only the emperor triumphed, and generals received triumphal honours instead.

pairs.source_text: Et hoc quidem virtutis praemium, illud solacium doloris accepit, quod filio eius Cottio, quem amisit absens, habitus est honor statuae. Rarum id in iuvene.
pairs.question: Cui Vestricii Spurinnae filio defuncto honor statuae publice habitus est?
pairs.question_en: Which dead son of Vestricius Spurinna was honoured with a public statue?
pairs.derivation: The rare public statue for a young man who had held no office, granted to Spurinna's son Cottius. Anchored to father and son by name; stated verbatim. Closed-book: public honorific statuary and its normal restriction to men of achievement is shared civic knowledge.

pairs.source_text: Studes an piscaris an venaris an simul omnia? Possunt enim omnia simul fieri ad Larium nostrum. Nam lacus piscem, feras silvae quibus lacus cingitur, studia altissimus iste secessus affatim suggerunt.
pairs.question: Ad quem lacum, ut Plinius scribit, studia, piscatus, venatio simul exerceri possunt?
pairs.question_en: Beside which lake, as Pliny writes, can study, fishing and hunting all be pursued at once?
pairs.derivation: Lacus Larius (Como), Pliny's home lake. Anchored to Pliny + the named lake; stated verbatim. Closed-book geography: the Larius is the lake of Comum and a recurring setting in the Epistulae.

pairs.source_text: Ego Sexto latum clavum a Caesare nostro, ego quaesturam impetravi; meo suffragio pervenit ad ius tribunatus petendi.
pairs.question: Quae duo Plinius Sexto Erucio a principe impetravit?
pairs.question_en: Which two things did Pliny obtain from the emperor for Sextus Erucius?
pairs.answer_en: The broad stripe and the quaestorship.
pairs.derivation: The latus clavus (admission to senatorial rank) and the quaestorship as the first steps of the cursus honorum, secured through a patron. Anchored to Pliny + Sextus Erucius; both stated verbatim. Closed-book institutional fact about senatorial careers.

pairs.source_text: Marius Priscus accusantibus Afris quibus pro consule praefuit, omissa defensione iudices petiit. Ego et Cornelius Tacitus, adesse provincialibus iussi, existimavimus fidei nostrae convenire notum senatui facere excessisse Priscum immanitate et saevitia crimina quibus dari iudices possent.
pairs.question: Qui duo advocati senatus iussu Afris contra Marium Priscum adfuerunt?
pairs.question_en: Which two advocates were ordered by the senate to act for the Africans against Marius Priscus?
pairs.derivation: The great repetundae trial of Marius Priscus, proconsul of Africa, prosecuted by Pliny and Tacitus. Anchored to the named defendant and province; both advocates named verbatim. Closed-book: this is the most famous senatorial trial of Trajan's reign.

pairs.source_text: Dixi horis paene quinque; nam duodecim clepsydris, quas spatiosissimas acceperam, sunt additae quattuor.
pairs.question: Quot clepsydris Plinius in causa Mari Prisci apud senatum usus est?
pairs.question_en: How many water-clocks did Pliny use in his speech against Marius Priscus before the senate?
pairs.derivation: The clepsydra as the measure of speaking time in Roman courts and senate. Anchored to Pliny + the Priscus trial; the numbers are stated verbatim. Closed-book and culturally salient: allotting an advocate so many clepsydrae is the standard Roman procedure.

pairs.source_text: Utcumque tamen animum cogitationemque collegi, coepi dicere non minore audientium assensu quam sollicitudine mea. Dixi horis paene quinque.
pairs.question: Quam diu Plinius in causa Mari Prisci dixisse se scribit?
pairs.question_en: For how long does Pliny write that he spoke in the case of Marius Priscus?
pairs.derivation: The length of Pliny's speech in the Priscus trial. Anchored to Pliny + the named case; stated verbatim. Closed-book: the marathon senatorial pleading is a memorable fact of Roman forensic practice.

pairs.source_text: Dilata res est in proximum senatum, cuius ipse conspectus augustissimus fuit. Princeps praesidebat, erat enim consul, ad hoc Ianuarius mensis cum cetera tum praecipue senatorum frequentia celeberrimus.
pairs.question: Quo mense causa Mari Prisci in senatu praesidente principe acta est?
pairs.question_en: In which month was the case of Marius Priscus heard in the senate with the emperor presiding?
pairs.derivation: The trial held in January, when the senate is fullest, with the emperor presiding as consul. Anchored to the named trial; the month is stated verbatim. Closed-book: January as the month of maximum senatorial attendance is a fact of Roman public life.

pairs.source_text: Princeps praesidebat, erat enim consul, ad hoc Ianuarius mensis cum cetera tum praecipue senatorum frequentia celeberrimus.
pairs.question: Quo munere fungens princeps senatui in causa Mari Prisci praesedit?
pairs.question_en: In what office was the emperor presiding over the senate in the trial of Marius Priscus?
pairs.derivation: The emperor presiding over the senate because he was that year's consul. Anchored to the named trial; stated verbatim. Closed-book constitutional fact: the princeps presides in the senate by virtue of the consulship, not by mere primacy.

pairs.source_text: Venerunt qui adesse erant iussi, Vitellius Honoratus et Flavius Marcianus; ex quibus Honoratus trecentis milibus exsilium equitis Romani septemque amicorum eius ultimam poenam, Marcianus unius equitis Romani septingentis milibus plura supplicia arguebatur emisse.
pairs.question: Quanti Vitellius Honoratus exsilium equitis Romani septemque amicorum eius supplicium emisse arguebatur?
pairs.question_en: For how much was Vitellius Honoratus charged with having bought a Roman knight's exile and the execution of seven of his friends?
pairs.derivation: The purchase of condemnations from the proconsul Priscus. Anchored to the named man and the named crime; the sum is stated verbatim. Closed-book: the sale of justice by provincial governors is the core of the repetundae law.

pairs.source_text: Cornutus Tertullus consul designatus, vir egregius et pro veritate firmissimus, censuit septingenta milia quae acceperat Marius aerario inferenda, Mario urbe Italiaque interdicendum, Marciano hoc amplius Africa.
pairs.question: Quantam pecuniam Marius Priscus ex senatus consulto aerario inferre iussus est?
pairs.question_en: How much money was Marius Priscus ordered by the senate's decree to pay into the treasury?
pairs.derivation: The sentence in the Priscus trial. Anchored to the named defendant; the sum is stated verbatim. Closed-book: repayment into the aerarium plus banishment is the classic penalty in a repetundae case.

pairs.source_text: censuit septingenta milia quae acceperat Marius aerario inferenda, Mario urbe Italiaque interdicendum, Marciano hoc amplius Africa.
pairs.question: Qua poena praeter pecuniam Marius Priscus multatus est?
pairs.question_en: With what penalty besides the money was Marius Priscus punished?
pairs.answer_en: He was banned from Rome and Italy.
pairs.derivation: Interdiction from Rome and Italy, the standard senatorial banishment. Anchored to the named defendant; stated verbatim. Closed-book penal-law fact of the principate.

pairs.source_text: Obversabatur praeter illa quae supra dixi causae difficultas: stabat modo consularis, modo septemvir epulonum, iam neutrum.
pairs.question: Quo sacerdotio Marius Priscus ante damnationem functus erat?
pairs.question_en: Which priesthood had Marius Priscus held before his condemnation?
pairs.derivation: The septemviri epulonum, one of the four great priestly colleges of Rome, forfeited on condemnation. Anchored to the named defendant; stated verbatim. Closed-book: the epulones are a standard item of Roman sacral institutions.

pairs.source_text: Huius actionem vespera inclusit, non tamen sic ut abrumperet. Itaque in tertium diem probationes exierunt. Iam hoc ipsum pulchrum et antiquum, senatum nocte dirimi, triduo vocari, triduo contineri.
pairs.question: Per quot dies senatus in causa Mari Prisci continuatus est?
pairs.question_en: For how many days did the senate sit continuously on the case of Marius Priscus?
pairs.derivation: The three-day senatorial hearing, broken off each night at dusk. Anchored to the named trial; stated verbatim. Closed-book procedural fact: the senate could not sit after nightfall, so a great case ran over successive days.

pairs.source_text: stipulatusque de Marciano quinquaginta milia denariorum probabatur, ipse praeterea accepisse sestertia decem milia foedissimo quidem titulo, nomine unguentarii.
pairs.question: Quo foedissimo titulo Hostilius Firminus decem milia sestertium accepisse probabatur?
pairs.question_en: Under what shameful heading was Hostilius Firminus shown to have taken ten thousand sesterces?
pairs.derivation: The bribe entered in the accounts as an item for unguents. Anchored to the named legate; stated verbatim. Closed-book: the detail is the memorable sting of the Priscus affair, and the account-book entry (titulus) is a real feature of Roman documentary practice.

pairs.source_text: Firminus inductus in senatum respondit crimini noto. Secutae sunt diversae sententiae consulum designatorum. Cornutus Tertullus censuit ordine movendum, Acutius Nerva in sortitione provinciae rationem eius non habendam. Quae sententia tamquam mitior vicit.
pairs.question: Quam poenam senatus in Hostilium Firminum tandem statuit?
pairs.answer: Ut in sortitione provinciae ratio eius non haberetur.
pairs.question_en: What penalty did the senate finally impose on Hostilius Firminus?
pairs.answer_en: That he should be passed over in the allotment of provinces.
pairs.derivation: The milder sentence: not expulsion from the senate, but exclusion from the sortitio provinciarum. Anchored to the named man; stated verbatim. Closed-book institutional fact: senatorial provinces were assigned by lot among ex-magistrates.

pairs.source_text: Sed hoc pluribus visum est. Numerantur enim sententiae, non ponderantur; nec aliud in publico consilio potest fieri, in quo nihil est tam inaequale quam aequalitas ipsa.
pairs.question: Cuius auctoris est illud de senatus suffragiis dictum, 'numerantur sententiae, non ponderantur'?
pairs.question_en: Which author wrote the saying about senatorial votes, 'votes are counted, not weighed'?
pairs.derivation: The much-quoted maxim on voting in a deliberative body. Anchored to its author and its subject (the senate's division); quoted verbatim. Closed-book: 'numerantur sententiae, non ponderantur' circulates as a Latin tag.

pairs.source_text: Is erit Voconius Romanus. Pater ei in equestri gradu clarus, clarior vitricu, immo pater alius, nam huic quoque nomini pietate successit, mater e primi. Ipse citerioris Hispaniae, scis quod iudicium provinciae illius, quanta sit gravitas, flamen proxime fuit.
pairs.question: Cuius provinciae flamen fuit Voconius Romanus?
pairs.question_en: Of which province was Voconius Romanus flamen?
pairs.derivation: The provincial flaminate, the priesthood of the imperial cult held by the leading man of a province's assembly. Anchored to the named man; stated verbatim. Closed-book institutional fact of provincial religion and honour.

pairs.source_text: Equidem iuvenis statim iuveni, quantum potui per aetatem, avidissime contuli, et nuper ab optimo principe trium liberorum ius impetravi; quod quamquam parce et cum delectu daret, mihi tamen tamquam eligeret indulsit.
pairs.question: Quod ius Plinius Voconio Romano ab optimo principe impetravit?
pairs.question_en: What right did Pliny obtain from the emperor for Voconius Romanus?
pairs.derivation: The ius trium liberorum, the privilege of the Augustan marriage legislation, granted by imperial favour to the childless. Anchored to Pliny + Voconius Romanus; stated verbatim. Closed-book: it is one of the best-known privileges of Roman law and society.

pairs.source_text: Inde iam non inurbane 'Sophokleis' vocantur 'apo tou sophôs kai kaleisthai', isdem Latinum nomen impositum est Laudiceni.
pairs.question: Quo nomine Latino conducti laudatores in basilica appellabantur?
pairs.question_en: By what Latin name were the hired applauders in the basilica called?
pairs.derivation: The nickname for those who applauded advocates for a dinner or a fee. Anchored to the centumviral court; the term is stated verbatim. Closed-book and culturally salient: the claque of the Roman courts is a recognized social phenomenon.

pairs.source_text: Here duo nomenclatores mei, habent sane aetatem eorum qui nuper togas sumpserint, ternis denariis ad laudandum trahebantur.
pairs.question: Quanto pretio nomenclatores Plinii ad laudandum in basilica trahebantur?
pairs.question_en: For what price were Pliny's nomenclators being drawn in to applaud in the basilica?
pairs.derivation: The going rate paid to a hired applauder. Anchored to Pliny's own household slaves and the basilica; the price is stated verbatim. Closed-book: prices and the practice of paid applause are exactly the ambient economic detail of Roman city life.

pairs.source_text: Here duo nomenclatores mei, habent sane aetatem eorum qui nuper togas sumpserint, ternis denariis ad laudandum trahebantur. Tanti constat ut sis disertissimus. Hoc pretio quamlibet numerosa subsellia implentur, hoc ingens corona colligitur, hoc infiniti clamores commoventur, cum mesochorus dedit signum.
pairs.question: Quo dato signo corona conducta in basilica clamores tollebat?
pairs.question_en: At whose signal did the hired ring of listeners raise its shouts in the basilica?
pairs.answer_en: At the signal of the mesochorus (the chorus-leader).
pairs.derivation: The claque directed by a mesochorus, as in the theatre. Anchored to the centumviral court; stated verbatim. Closed-book: organized applause with a leader is a well-known institution of Roman public performance.

pairs.source_text: Sequuntur auditores actoribus similes, conducti et redempti. Manceps convenitur; in media basilica tam palam sportulae quam in triclinio dantur; ex iudicio in iudicium pari mercede transitur.
pairs.question: Quid conductis auditoribus in media basilica tam palam quam in triclinio dabatur?
pairs.question_en: What was handed out to the hired listeners in the middle of the basilica as openly as at a dinner-table?
pairs.derivation: The sportula, the client's dole, paid here to hired applauders. Anchored to the basilica scene; stated verbatim. Closed-book and highly salient: the sportula is the emblematic transaction of Roman patronage.

pairs.source_text: Primus hunc audiendi morem induxit Larcius Licinus, hactenus tamen ut auditores corrogaret. Ita certe ex Quintiliano praeceptore meo audisse me memini.
pairs.question: Quis primus morem conducendi auditores in iudicia induxisse dicitur?
pairs.question_en: Who is said to have first introduced the practice of rounding up listeners for the courts?
pairs.derivation: The origin of the paid audience, reported to Pliny by Quintilian. Anchored to the named innovator; stated verbatim. Closed-book: the beginnings of the courtroom claque are a shared piece of rhetorical-historical lore.

pairs.source_text: Ita certe ex Quintiliano praeceptore meo audisse me memini.
pairs.question: Quem rhetorem praeceptorem suum Plinius nominat?
pairs.question_en: Which rhetorician does Pliny name as his own teacher?
pairs.derivation: Pliny's schooling under Quintilian. Anchored to Pliny; stated verbatim (Quintiliano praeceptore meo). Closed-book: that the author of the Institutio taught Pliny is a standard fact of Latin literary history.

pairs.source_text: Narrabat ille: 'Assectabar Domitium Afrum. Cum apud centumviros diceret graviter et lente, hoc enim illi actionis genus erat, audit ex proximo immodicum insolitumque clamorem. Admiratus reticuit; ubi silentium factum est, repetit quod abruperat. Iterum clamor, iterum reticuit, et post silentium coepit. Idem tertio. Novissime quis diceret quaesiit. Responsum est: "Licinus." Tum intermissa causa "Centumviri," inquit, "hoc artificium periit."'
pairs.question: Quis orator apud centumviros dicens exclamavit 'hoc artificium periit'?
pairs.question_en: Which orator, pleading before the centumviri, exclaimed 'this art is dead'?
pairs.derivation: Domitius Afer's famous protest at the rise of the hired claque, transmitted through Quintilian. Anchored to the named orator + the centumviral court; quoted verbatim. Closed-book: Domitius Afer is a canonical orator of the early empire and this is his best-remembered mot.

pairs.source_text: Tu quidem pro cetera tua diligentia admones me codicillos Aciliani, qui me ex parte instituit heredem, pro non scriptis habendos, quia non sint confirmati testamento; quod ius ne mihi quidem ignotum est.
pairs.question: Quid iure fiebat de codicillis testamento non confirmatis?
pairs.question_en: What, in law, became of codicils not confirmed by a will?
pairs.answer_en: They were treated as if unwritten.
pairs.derivation: The rule of Roman succession law on unconfirmed codicilli. Anchored to the named legal instrument and Pliny's inheritance from Acilianus; stated verbatim. Closed-book: wills, codicils and their formal requirements are core Roman legal culture.

pairs.source_text: Decem septem milibus passuum ab urbe secessit, ut peractis quae agenda fuerint salvo iam et composito die possis ibi manere.
pairs.question: Quot milibus passuum Laurentinum Plinii ab urbe Roma distat?
pairs.question_en: How many miles from Rome is Pliny's Laurentine villa?
pairs.derivation: The distance of the Laurentine villa from Rome. Anchored to Pliny + his named villa; the number is stated verbatim. Closed-book: the Laurentinum is the most famous described villa in Latin literature, and its nearness to Rome is the point of the description.

pairs.source_text: Aditur non una via; nam et Laurentina et Ostiensis eodem ferunt, sed Laurentina a quarto decimo lapide, Ostiensis ab undecimo relinquenda est.
pairs.question: A quoto lapide viae Laurentina et Ostiensis relinquendae sunt ei qui Laurentinum Plinii petit?
pairs.answer: Laurentina a quarto decimo, Ostiensis ab undecimo.
pairs.question_en: At which milestone must the Laurentine and the Ostian roads be left by someone making for Pliny's Laurentine villa?
pairs.answer_en: The Laurentina at the fourteenth, the Ostiensis at the eleventh.
pairs.derivation: The two approach roads and the milestones at which one turns off. Anchored to the named roads + the named villa; both numbers stated verbatim. Closed-book: the via Ostiensis and via Laurentina and the Roman milestone system are shared topographical knowledge.

pairs.source_text: In hanc ego diaetam cum me recepi, abesse mihi etiam a villa mea videor, magnamque eius voluptatem praecipue Saturnalibus capio, cum reliqua pars tecti licentia dierum festisque clamoribus personat; nam nec ipse meorum lusibus nec illi studiis meis obstrepunt.
pairs.question: Quo festo praecipue Plinius secessu diaetae suae Laurentinae fruebatur, cum reliqua villa clamoribus personaret?
pairs.question_en: At which festival above all did Pliny enjoy the seclusion of his private suite at the Laurentine villa, while the rest of the house rang with shouting?
pairs.derivation: The licence of the Saturnalia in a Roman household, with the slaves' games filling the house. Anchored to Pliny + his villa; the festival is named verbatim and its 'licentia dierum' described. Closed-book: the Saturnalia and its household misrule are prime Roman festival knowledge.

pairs.source_text: Suggerunt affatim ligna proximae silvae; ceteras copias ostiensis colonia ministrat. Frugi quidem homini sufficit etiam vicus, quem una villa discernit. In hoc balinea meritoria tria, magna commoditas.
pairs.question: Quot balinea meritoria in vico prope Laurentinum Plinii erant?
pairs.question_en: How many public bath-houses for hire were there in the village near Pliny's Laurentine villa?
pairs.derivation: The three hired baths in the neighbouring village, a convenience when heating one's own bath was not worth it. Anchored to the named villa; the number is stated verbatim. Closed-book: balnea meritoria, the small commercial baths, are a standard feature of Italian settlements.

pairs.source_text: Suggerunt affatim ligna proximae silvae; ceteras copias ostiensis colonia ministrat.
pairs.question: Quae colonia Laurentino Plinii ceteras copias ministrabat?
pairs.question_en: Which colony supplied Pliny's Laurentine villa with its other provisions?
pairs.derivation: Ostia as the market for the Laurentine coast. Anchored to the named villa + the named colony; stated verbatim. Closed-book: Ostia is the port-colony of Rome and a fixture of Italian geography.

pairs.source_text: Mare non sane pretiosis piscibus abundat, soleas tamen et squillas optimas egerit.
pairs.question: Quae duo maris animalia optima ante Laurentinum Plinii capiebantur?
pairs.question_en: Which two excellent sea-creatures were taken off Pliny's Laurentine shore?
pairs.derivation: The catch of the Laurentine coast, poor in luxury fish but good for sole and prawn. Anchored to the named villa; both named verbatim. Closed-book food fact: soleae and squillae are standard items of the Roman fish market.

pairs.source_text: Gestatio buxo aut rore marino, ubi deficit buxus, ambitur; nam buxus, qua parte defenditur tectis, abunde viret; aperto caelo apertoque vento et quamquam longinqua aspergine maris inarescit.
pairs.question: Quibus duobus fruticibus gestatio Laurentini Plinii cingebatur?
pairs.question_en: With which two shrubs was the drive at Pliny's Laurentine villa bordered?
pairs.answer_en: With box, or rosemary where the box failed.
pairs.derivation: Box hedging, replaced by rosemary where sea-spray killed it. Anchored to the named villa's gestatio; both plants named verbatim. Closed-book garden fact: clipped box is the signature planting of the Roman villa garden.

pairs.source_text: Verania Pisonis graviter iacebat, huius dico Pisonis, quem Galba adoptavit. Ad hanc Regulus venit. Primum impudentiam hominis, qui venerit ad aegram, cuius marito inimicissimus, ipsi invisissimus fuerat!
pairs.question: Cuius uxor fuit Verania, quam Regulus aegram adiit?
pairs.question_en: Whose wife was Verania, whom Regulus visited on her sickbed?
pairs.answer_en: Of the Piso whom Galba adopted.
pairs.derivation: Verania, widow of Piso Licinianus, Galba's adopted heir killed in AD 69. Anchored to Verania + Galba; stated verbatim. Closed-book: Galba's adoption of Piso is a famous episode of the year of the four emperors.

pairs.source_text: at ille etiam proximus toro sedit, quo die qua hora nata esset interrogavit. Ubi audiit, componit vultum intendit oculos movet labra, agitat digitos computat. Nihil. Ut diu miseram exspectatione suspendit, 'habes' inquit 'climacterium tempus sed evades. Quod ut tibi magis liqueat, haruspicem consulam, quem sum frequenter expertus.' Nec mora, sacrificium facit, affirmat exta cum siderum significatione congruere.
pairs.question: Quem vatem Regulus consuluit ut Veraniae aegrae fidem de sideribus faceret?
pairs.question_en: Which kind of diviner did Regulus consult to make the sick Verania believe what the stars said?
pairs.derivation: Astrological calculation of the birth-hour backed by a haruspex's inspection of entrails. Anchored to Regulus + Verania; stated verbatim. Closed-book: the haruspex and the climacteric year are core items of Roman divinatory culture.

pairs.source_text: Aurelia ornata femina signatura testamentum sumpserat pulcherrimas tunicas. Regulus cum venisset ad signandum, 'Rogo' inquit 'has mihi leges.' Aurelia ludere hominem putabat, ille serio instabat; ne multa, coegit mulierem aperire tabulas ac sibi tunicas quas erat induta legare.
pairs.question: Quid Regulus Aureliam testamentum signaturam sibi legare coegit?
pairs.question_en: What did Regulus compel Aurelia, as she was about to seal her will, to leave him?
pairs.derivation: The notorious anecdote of Regulus and Aurelia's tunics. Anchored to the two named persons; stated verbatim. Closed-book and culturally salient: the sealing of wills before witnesses, and captatio, are Roman institutions, and this is the emblematic story of the legacy-hunter.

pairs.source_text: Velleius Blaesus ille locuples consularis novissima valetudine conflictabatur: cupiebat mutare testamentum. Regulus qui speraret aliquid ex novis tabulis, quia nuper captare eum coeperat, medicos hortari rogare, quoquo modo spiritum homini prorogarent.
pairs.question: Quo artificio Regulus, ut Plinius narrat, opes suas ex alienis testamentis augebat?
pairs.question_en: By what practice, as Pliny relates, did Regulus increase his wealth out of other people's wills?
pairs.derivation: Captatio, the courting of the childless and the dying for legacies. Anchored to Regulus and the named victims; the verb captare is used verbatim of him. Closed-book: legacy-hunting is one of the most-discussed social vices of imperial Rome (Horace, Petronius, Juvenal).

pairs.source_text: Aspice Regulum, qui ex paupere et tenui ad tantas opes per flagitia processit, ut ipse mihi dixerit, cum consuleret quam cito sestertium sescentiens impleturus esset, invenisse se exta duplicia, quibus portendi miliens et ducentiens habiturum.
pairs.question: Quantam pecuniam Regulo exta duplicia portendere visa sunt?
pairs.question_en: How much money did the doubled entrails seem to portend for Regulus?
pairs.answer_en: One hundred and twenty million sesterces.
pairs.derivation: The doubled entrails read as doubling Regulus' hoped-for sixty million. Anchored to Regulus; both sums stated verbatim. Closed-book: extispicy and the reading of doubled organs as a doubling omen belong to Roman divinatory practice.

pairs.source_text: Mane lectulo continetur, hora secunda calceos poscit, ambulat milia passuum tria nec minus animum quam corpus exercet.
pairs.question: Qua hora Spurinna, cuius vitae ordinem Plinius describit, calceos poscere solebat?
pairs.question_en: At what hour did Spurinna, whose daily order Pliny describes, call for his shoes?
pairs.derivation: Spurinna's ordered day, the classic Roman description of a well-regulated old age. Anchored to the named man; the hour is stated verbatim. Closed-book: reckoning the day by numbered hours from sunrise is basic Roman time-culture.

pairs.source_text: hora secunda calceos poscit, ambulat milia passuum tria nec minus animum quam corpus exercet.
pairs.question: Quot milia passuum Spurinna mane ambulare solebat?
pairs.question_en: How many miles did Spurinna walk in the morning?
pairs.derivation: The three-mile morning walk in Spurinna's regimen. Anchored to the named man; the number is stated verbatim. Closed-book: the walk, ride and ball-game are the recognized Roman exercise regime.

pairs.source_text: Peractis septem milibus passuum iterum ambulat mille, iterum residit vel se cubiculo ac stilo reddit.
pairs.question: Quot milia passuum Spurinna vehiculo peragebat, antequam iterum mille ambularet?
pairs.question_en: How many miles did Spurinna cover by carriage before walking another mile?
pairs.derivation: The seven-mile drive of Spurinna's afternoon. Anchored to the named man; the number is stated verbatim. Closed-book: gestatio, the ride taken for health, is a standard Roman practice.

pairs.source_text: Ubi hora balinei nuntiata est, est autem hieme nona, aestate octava, in sole, si caret vento, ambulat nudus. Deinde movetur pila vehementer et diu.
pairs.question: Qua hora Spurinnae balineum hieme, qua aestate nuntiabatur?
pairs.question_en: At what hour was Spurinna's bath announced in winter, and at what hour in summer?
pairs.answer_en: At the ninth in winter, the eighth in summer.
pairs.derivation: The bathing hour, earlier in summer than in winter. Anchored to the named man; both hours stated verbatim. Closed-book and strongly salient: the hour of the bath before dinner is a defining rhythm of Roman daily life.

pairs.source_text: Deinde movetur pila vehementer et diu; nam hoc quoque exercitationis genere pugnat cum senectute. Lotus accubat et paulisper cibum differt.
pairs.question: Quo genere exercitationis Spurinna ante balineum cum senectute pugnabat?
pairs.question_en: By what kind of exercise did Spurinna fight off old age before his bath?
pairs.derivation: The ball-game taken before bathing. Anchored to the named man; stated verbatim. Closed-book: the pila before the bath is the standard Roman exercise, familiar from the baths themselves (sphaeristerium).

pairs.source_text: Apponitur cena non minus nitida quam frugi, in argento puro et antiquo; sunt in usu et Corinthia, quibus delectatur nec afficitur.
pairs.question: Quo genere vasorum praeter argentum purum Spurinna in cena utebatur?
pairs.question_en: What kind of vessels besides plain silver were used at Spurinna's dinner?
pairs.derivation: Corinthium aes, the most prized collector's bronze at Rome. Anchored to the named man's table; stated verbatim. Closed-book: Corinthian bronze is a byword for connoisseurship (cf. Pliny the Elder, Petronius).

pairs.source_text: Frequenter comoedis cena distinguitur, ut voluptates quoque studiis condiantur.
pairs.question: Quibus artificibus cena Spurinnae frequenter distinguebatur?
pairs.question_en: By what performers was Spurinna's dinner often punctuated?
pairs.derivation: Comoedi performing between courses. Anchored to the named man's dinners; stated verbatim. Closed-book: dinner-table performance by comoedi is a recognized convention of the Roman convivium.

pairs.source_text: Scribit enim et quidem utraque lingua lyrica doctissima; mira illis dulcedo, mira suavitas, mira hilaritas.
pairs.question: Quod carminum genus et quibus linguis Spurinna scribebat?
pairs.question_en: What kind of poems, and in which languages, did Spurinna write?
pairs.derivation: Bilingual lyric composition by a Roman consular. Anchored to the named man; stated verbatim. Closed-book: the Roman elite's writing of Greek as well as Latin verse is shared cultural knowledge.

pairs.source_text: Inde illi post septimum et septuagensimum annum aurium oculorum vigor integer, inde agile et vividum corpus solaque ex senectute prudentia.
pairs.question: Quem annum aetatis Spurinna egressus integrum adhuc aurium oculorumque vigorem retinebat?
pairs.question_en: Past what year of his life did Spurinna still keep the full vigour of ears and eyes?
pairs.derivation: Spurinna's age and undiminished faculties. Anchored to the named man; the number is stated verbatim. Closed-book biographical fact about a celebrated consular of Trajan's day.

pairs.source_text: Arrianus Maturus Altinatium est princeps; cum dico princeps, non de facultatibus loquor, quae illi large supersunt, sed de castitate iustitia, gravitate prudentia.
pairs.question: Cuius municipii principem Plinius Arrianum Maturum appellat?
pairs.question_en: Of which town does Pliny call Arrianus Maturus the leading man?
pairs.derivation: Arrianus Maturus, chief man of Altinum in Venetia, who deliberately stayed in the equestrian order. Anchored to the named man; the town is named verbatim. Closed-book: the local princeps who declines senatorial rank is a recognized social type of Italy.

pairs.source_text: Iam studia eius extra limen proferenda sunt, iam circumspiciendus rhetor Latinus, cuius scholae severitas pudor in primis castitas constet. Adest enim adulescenti nostro cum ceteris naturae fortunaeque dotibus eximia corporis pulchritudo, cui in hoc lubrico aetatis non praeceptor modo sed custos etiam rectorque quaerendus est. Videor ergo demonstrare tibi posse Iulium Genitorem.
pairs.question: Quem rhetorem Latinum Plinius Corelliae Hispullae filio praeceptorem commendavit?
pairs.question_en: Which Latin rhetorician did Pliny recommend as teacher for the son of Corellia Hispulla?
pairs.derivation: The choice of a rhetor Latinus when a boy's studies move beyond the household tutor. Anchored to the named mother and teacher; stated verbatim. Closed-book: the progression from praeceptores domi to the school of rhetoric is the standard Roman educational ladder.

pairs.source_text: Cum publicum opus mea pecunia incohaturus in Tuscos excucurrissem, accepto ut praefectus aerari commeatu, legati provinciae Baeticae, questuri de proconsulatu Caecili Classici, advocatum me a senatu petiverunt.
pairs.question: Quod officium Plinius gerebat, cum legati Baeticae eum advocatum a senatu petiverunt?
pairs.question_en: What office was Pliny holding when the envoys of Baetica asked the senate for him as their advocate?
pairs.derivation: Pliny as praefectus aerarii Saturni, needing formal leave (commeatus) to travel. Anchored to Pliny + the Baetican embassy; stated verbatim. Closed-book: the treasury prefecture is a well-known senatorial post in Pliny's cursus.

pairs.source_text: Legati rursus inducti iterum me iam praesentem advocatum postulaverunt, implorantes fidem meam quam essent contra Massam Baebium experti, allegantes patrocini foedus.
pairs.question: Contra quem reum Plinius antea Baeticis adfuerat?
pairs.question_en: Against which defendant had Pliny previously acted for the people of Baetica?
pairs.derivation: Pliny's earlier prosecution of Baebius Massa for the Baeticans, the case also famous from Tacitus' Agricola. Anchored to Pliny + the province; the name is stated verbatim. Closed-book: Baebius Massa is one of the notorious informers and governors of the Domitianic age.

pairs.source_text: 'De iaculatione equestri unus'; hunc cum praefectus alae militaret, pari ingenio curaque composuit.
pairs.question: Quo munere militari fungens Plinius maior librum 'De iaculatione equestri' composuit?
pairs.question_en: While holding what military command did the elder Pliny compose his book On Throwing the Javelin from Horseback?
pairs.answer_en: As prefect of a cavalry wing.
pairs.derivation: The elder Pliny's first book, written on campaign as commander of a cavalry ala. Anchored to the named author and title; stated verbatim. Closed-book: the catalogue of the elder Pliny's works is a standard piece of Roman literary history.

pairs.source_text: 'De vita Pomponi Secundi duo'; a quo singulariter amatus hoc memoriae amici quasi debitum munus exsolvit.
pairs.question: Cuius amici vitam Plinius maior duobus libris complexus est?
pairs.question_en: Whose life did the elder Pliny cover in two books?
pairs.derivation: The elder Pliny's biography of his friend the tragedian and consular Pomponius Secundus. Anchored to author and subject; stated verbatim. Closed-book: it is a fixed item in the canonical list of the elder Pliny's writings.

pairs.source_text: 'Bellorum Germaniae viginti'; quibus omnia quae cum Germanis gessimus bella collegit.
pairs.question: Quot libris Plinius maior bella Germaniae complexus est?
pairs.question_en: In how many books did the elder Pliny cover the German wars?
pairs.derivation: The twenty books of the Bella Germaniae, the lost history used by Tacitus. Anchored to the named author + title; the number is stated verbatim. Closed-book: this is the best-known lost work of the elder Pliny.

pairs.source_text: Incohavit cum in Germania militaret, somnio monitus: astitit ei quiescenti Drusi Neronis effigies, qui Germaniae latissime victor ibi periit, commendabat memoriam suam orabatque ut se ab iniuria oblivionis assereret.
pairs.question: Cuius ducis effigies Plinio maiori per somnium astitit, ut bella Germaniae scriberet?
pairs.question_en: Whose likeness stood over the elder Pliny in a dream, prompting him to write the German wars?
pairs.derivation: The dream-apparition of Drusus, conqueror of Germany, who died there. Anchored to the elder Pliny + Drusus; stated verbatim. Closed-book: Drusus' German campaigns and death are canonical early-imperial history, and the dream is the famous origin-story of the work.

pairs.source_text: 'Studiosi tres', in sex volumina propter amplitudinem divisi, quibus oratorem ab incunabulis instituit et perficit.
pairs.question: In quot volumina 'Studiosi' libri tres Plini maioris propter amplitudinem divisi sunt?
pairs.question_en: Into how many rolls were the three books of the elder Pliny's Studiosus divided because of their bulk?
pairs.derivation: The Studiosus, a training of the orator from the cradle, in three books split over six rolls. Anchored to the named author + title; the number is stated verbatim. Closed-book: the distinction between liber and volumen is real Roman book-culture.

pairs.source_text: 'Dubii sermonis octo': scripsit sub Nerone novissimis annis, cum omne studiorum genus paulo liberius et erectius periculosum servitus fecisset.
pairs.question: Sub quo principe Plinius maior octo libros 'Dubii sermonis' composuit?
pairs.question_en: Under which emperor did the elder Pliny compose the eight books of Dubius Sermo?
pairs.derivation: The grammatical work written in Nero's last years, when safer subjects were prudent. Anchored to author, title and emperor; stated verbatim. Closed-book: the retreat into harmless scholarship under a dangerous prince is a well-known feature of Neronian literary history.

pairs.source_text: 'A fine Aufidi Bassi triginta unus.' 'Naturae historiarum triginta septem', opus diffusum eruditum, nec minus varium quam ipsa natura.
pairs.question: Cuius historici opus Plinius maior triginta uno libris continuavit?
pairs.question_en: Whose historical work did the elder Pliny continue in thirty-one books?
pairs.derivation: The lost continuation 'A fine Aufidi Bassi', the history used by Tacitus. Anchored to the named author + predecessor; stated verbatim. Closed-book: the chain of imperial historians from Aufidius Bassus to Pliny is standard literary history.

pairs.source_text: 'Naturae historiarum triginta septem', opus diffusum eruditum, nec minus varium quam ipsa natura.
pairs.question: Quot libris Naturalis historia Plini maioris constat?
pairs.question_en: Of how many books does the elder Pliny's Natural History consist?
pairs.derivation: The thirty-seven books of the Naturalis Historia. Anchored to the named author + work; the number is stated verbatim. Closed-book: the extent of the encyclopaedia is among the most widely known facts of Latin letters.

pairs.source_text: Magis miraberis si scieris illum aliquamdiu causas actitasse, decessisse anno sexto et quinquagensimo, medium tempus distentum impeditumque qua officiis maximis qua amicitia principum egisse.
pairs.question: Quoto anno aetatis Plinius maior decessit?
pairs.question_en: In what year of his life did the elder Pliny die?
pairs.derivation: The elder Pliny's age at death (in the eruption of Vesuvius). Anchored to the named man; the number is stated verbatim. Closed-book biographical fact of a famous author.

pairs.source_text: Lucubrare Vulcanalibus incipiebat non auspicandi causa sed studendi statim a nocte multa, hieme vero ab hora septima vel cum tardissime octava, saepe sexta.
pairs.question: Quo festo Plinius maior lucubrationes suas incipere solebat?
pairs.question_en: At which festival did the elder Pliny begin his nightly studies by lamplight?
pairs.derivation: The Vulcanalia (23 August) as the customary start of the season of lamp-lit work. Anchored to the elder Pliny; the festival is named verbatim. Closed-book: the Vulcanalia is a named feast of the Roman calendar, and starting lucubratio then was a recognized custom.

pairs.source_text: Ante lucem ibat ad Vespasianum imperatorem, nam ille quoque noctibus utebatur, inde ad delegatum sibi officium.
pairs.question: Ad quem principem Plinius maior ante lucem salutatum ire solebat?
pairs.question_en: To which emperor did the elder Pliny go before daybreak to pay his respects?
pairs.derivation: The pre-dawn imperial salutatio, with Vespasian likewise working by night. Anchored to both named men; stated verbatim. Closed-book: the early-morning salutatio of patron and emperor is a defining Roman social ritual.

pairs.source_text: Nihil enim legit quod non excerperet; dicere etiam solebat nullum esse librum tam malum ut non aliqua parte prodesset.
pairs.question: Cuius auctoris dictum est nullum esse librum tam malum ut non aliqua parte prosit?
pairs.question_en: Which author's saying is it that no book is so bad as not to be useful in some part?
pairs.derivation: The famous dictum reported by his nephew. Anchored to the elder Pliny; quoted verbatim. Closed-book: 'nullus est liber tam malus...' is a standing Latin proverb.

pairs.source_text: In itinere quasi solutus ceteris curis, huic uni vacabat: ad latus notarius cum libro et pugillaribus, cuius manus hieme manicis muniebantur, ut ne caeli quidem asperitas ullum studii tempus eriperet; qua ex causa Romae quoque sella vehebatur.
pairs.question: Quibus manus notarii Plini maioris hieme muniebantur, ne studendi tempus periret?
pairs.question_en: With what were the hands of the elder Pliny's shorthand-writer protected in winter, so that no study-time should be lost?
pairs.derivation: The secretary taking dictation on the road, his hands sleeved against the cold. Anchored to the elder Pliny + his notarius; stated verbatim. Closed-book: dictation to a notarius is the standard Roman mode of composition, and this is its most famous illustration.

pairs.source_text: ut ne caeli quidem asperitas ullum studii tempus eriperet; qua ex causa Romae quoque sella vehebatur.
pairs.question: Quo vehiculo Plinius maior Romae vehebatur, ne studiis tempus deesset?
pairs.question_en: In what conveyance did the elder Pliny travel about Rome so as not to lose time for study?
pairs.derivation: The sella (litter-chair) used so that reading could continue in the streets. Anchored to the elder Pliny; stated verbatim. Closed-book: the sella and lectica are the standard means of getting about Rome for a man of rank.
